# Antiviral agents

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Relevant pharmacology > Antiviral agents*

[Original Article Link](/library/pm0Lgg)

---

## Summary

Antivirals are a class of medications that are used to treat viral infections. Most viral infections resolve spontaneously in immunocompetent individuals. The aim of antiviral therapy is to minimize symptoms and <u>infectivity</u> as well as to shorten the duration of illness. These drugs act by arresting the <u>viral replication cycle</u> at various stages. Currently, antiviral therapy is available only for a limited number of infections. Most of the antiviral drugs currently available are used to treat infections caused by <u>HIV</u>, herpes <u>viruses</u>, <u>hepatitis B</u> and C <u>viruses</u>, and <u>influenza A</u> and B <u>viruses</u>. Because <u>viruses</u> are obligate intracellular <u>parasites</u>, it is difficult to find drug targets that interfere with viral replication without also harming the host cells. Unlike other antimicrobials, antiviral drugs do not deactivate or destroy the microbe (in this case, the <u>virus</u>) but act by inhibiting replication. In this way, they prevent the viral load from increasing to a point where it could cause pathogenesis, allowing the body's innate immune mechanisms to neutralize the <u>virus</u>. This article provides an overview of the most commonly used antiviral agents. For more information on antiretroviral agents used in the treatment of <u>HIV</u>, which is known as <u>highly active antiretroviral therapy</u> (<u>HAART</u>), see “Overview of antiretrovirals for <u>HIV treatment</u>.”

## Overview

<u>Viruses</u> are <u>obligate pathogens</u>, which depend on host-cell machinery for replication. Most antiviral agents target key enzymes required for viral replication (see “<u>Viral life cycle</u>” for details).




| Overview of the <u>viral replication cycle</u> and targets of antiviral drug |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Viral replication cycle</u> | Target | Antiviral drug |
| Fusion with host cell | <br>* Attachment<br><br> | <br>* <u>CCR5-antagonist</u> (e.g., <u>maraviroc</u>)<br><br> |
| <br>* Penetration<br><br> | <br>* <u>Fusion inhibitor</u> (e.g., <u>enfuvirtide</u>)<br><br> |  |
| Uncoating | <br>* Release of <u>nucleic acid</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Amantadine</u><br><br> |
| Replication of <u>viral genome</u> | <br>* Reverse <u>transcription</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>NRTI</u> (e.g., <u>lamivudine</u>)<br><br>* <u>NNRTI</u> (e.g., <u>nevirapine</u>, <u>efavirenz</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>DNA</u> integration (<u>integrase</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Integrase inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>dolutegravir</u>, <u>elvitegravir</u>, <u>raltegravir</u>)<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Nucleic acid</u> synthesis (<u>DNA polymerase</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Guanosine</u> analogues (e.g., <u>acyclovir</u>, <u>ganciclovir</u>)<br><br>* Viral <u>DNA polymerase</u> inhibitors (e.g., <u>cidofovir</u>, <u>foscarnet</u>)<br><br>* <u>Guanine</u> <u>nucleotide</u> synthesis inhibitor (e.g., <u>ribavirin</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Protein synthesis</u> and assembly of viral components | <br>* <u>Protein synthesis</u> (<u>transcription</u> and <u>translation</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Interferon alpha</u><br><br> |
| <br>* Proteolytic processing (<u>protease</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Protease inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>atazanavir</u>, <u>darunavir</u>, <u>indinavir</u> for <u>HIV</u>, boceprevir for <u>HCV</u>)<br><br> |  |
| Release of new <u>viruses</u> from host cell | <br>* Viral <u>budding</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Neuraminidase inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>oseltamivir</u>, <u>zanamivir</u>)<br><br> |

## Antivirals against hepatitis B and C

See “<u>Antiviral treatment of chronic hepatitis C</u>” and “<u>Antiviral treatment of chronic hepatitis B</u>.”





### Antivirals against both <u>hepatitis</u> Band C




| <br>Overview of antivirals against both hepatitis B and C [[1]](/library/DnY1vp)[[2]](/library/XC09qR)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agents | Mechanism of action | Indications | Contraindications | Adverse effects |
| <br>Pegylated interferon alfa and interferon-α <br> | <br>* Antiviral and immunomodulatory effect via intercellular and intracellular mechanisms <br><br>* Inhibition of viral <u>protein synthesis</u><br><br>* Promotion of breakdown of viral <u>RNA</u><br><br>* Increased expression of <u>MHC class I</u> molecules<br><br> | <br><br>* Monotherapy in acute <u>hepatitis C</u> and chronic active <u>hepatitis B</u><br><br>* As a combination treatment  in chronic <u>hepatitis C</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Decompensated cirrhosis</u><br><br>* Psychiatric conditions<br><br>* <u>Pregnancy</u><br><br>* Autoimmune conditions<br><br>* <u>Leukopenia</u> or <u>thrombocytopenia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Flu-like</u> symptoms<br><br>* <u>Bone marrow suppression</u><br><br>* <u>CNS</u><br><br>* Depressive mood<br><br>* <u>Seizures</u><br><br>* Induction of <u>autoantibodies</u><br><br>* <u>Myopathy</u><br><br><br> |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agents | Mechanism of action | Indications | Adverse effects |
| <br>Tenofovir  Adefovir<br> | <br>* Nucleotide analogue (<u>adenosine</u> analogue): <u>phosphorylated</u> to triphosphate in hepatic cells (activation) → binds to viral <u>DNA polymerase</u> → premature termination of <u>DNA</u> <u>transcription</u><br><br> | <br>* Chronic active <u>hepatitis B</u>, <u>HIV</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Nephrotoxicity</u> (e.g., <u>Fanconi syndrome</u>)<br><br>* <u>Headache</u> and abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* Disease exacerbation is possible.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Entecavir Lamivudine Telbivudine<br> | <br>* <u>Nucleoside analogue</u>: inhibition of <u>reverse transcriptase</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Chronic active <u>hepatitis B</u><br><br>* <u>HIV</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Occasional<br><br>* Gastrointestinal symptoms<br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br>* <u>Headache</u><br><br>* Rare<br><br>* <u>Vasculitides</u><br><br>* Neuropathies<br><br>* <u>Neutropenia</u><br><br>* <u>Lactic acidosis</u><br><br><br> |

> [!TIP]
> <u>Protease inhibitors</u> used to treat <u>HIV</u> end in ”navir.” <u>Protease inhibitors</u> used to treat <u>HCV</u> end in “previr.”

## Antivirals against herpes viruses

| <br>Overview of antivirals against herpesviruses [[3]](/library/n3Y7QK)[[4]](/library/L3YwQK)[[5]](/library/o3Y0jK)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agents | Mechanism of action | Indications | Adverse effects | Mechanism of antiviral resistance |
| <br>Acyclovir Valacyclovir  Penciclovir Famciclovir <br> | <br><br>* <u>Guanosine</u> analogue (<u>nucleoside analogue</u>)<br><br>* <u>HSV</u>/<u>VZV</u>-coded thymidine kinase monophosphorylates the <u>guanosine</u> analogue to an active intermediate → <u>phosphorylation</u> by cellular <u>kinases</u> → <u>acyclovir</u> triphosphate (ACV-<u>TP</u>)<br><br>* The <u>phosphorylated</u> drug is incorporated into the replicating viral <u>DNA</u> strand → inhibition of viral <u>DNA polymerase</u> via chain termination<br><br>* Selective action in infected cells only with minimal effect on host cells → fewer side effects<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Active infection (not effective against <u>latent infections</u> )<br><br>* <u>Herpes simplex</u><br><br>* Systemic: <u>HSV encephalitis</u>, and <u>genital herpes</u><br><br>* Topical: early genital and mucocutaneous herpes<br><br>* <u>Varicella zoster</u>: (e.g., active <u>shingles</u>) treated with systemic <u>acyclovir</u>, especially in <u>immunocompromised</u> adults<br><br>* <u>EBV</u> (weak activity)<br><br>* Prophylaxis in <u>immunodeficient</u> and immunocompetent individuals with recurring or severe infections<br><br>* No effect on <u>CMV</u> (lacks <u>thymidine kinase</u> needed to activate the <u>guanosine</u> analogue)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Acyclovir</u><br><br>* Obstructive crystal-induced nephropathy<br><br>* <u>Acute kidney injury</u><br><br>* Both can be prevented by adequate hydration and dosage adjustment<br><br>* <u>Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura</u><br><br>* Gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., <u>nausea</u>)<br><br>* ↑ <u>Transaminases</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Mutation of viral <u>thymidine kinase</u><br><br> |
| <br>Ganciclovir Valganciclovir <br> | <br><br>* <u>Guanosine</u> analogue (<u>nucleoside analogue</u>)<br><br>* <u>Phosphorylation</u> to 5' monophosphate by the <u>CMV</u>-coded UL97 <u>kinase</u>  → further <u>phosphorylation</u> to triphosphate by cellular <u>kinases</u><br><br>* Incorporation of the <u>phosphorylated</u> drug into the replicating viral <u>DNA</u> strand → inhibition of viral <u>DNA polymerase</u> → termination of viral <u>DNA synthesis</u><br><br>* Lower selectivity than <u>acyclovir</u> and <u>penciclovir</u> → inhibition of host cells' <u>DNA replication</u> → higher toxicity<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Systemic treatment of choice for <u>CMV retinitis</u> in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients (e.g., patients with <u>AIDS</u>)<br><br>* <u>CMV</u> prophylaxis in transplant recipients<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Myelotoxicity: <u>pancytopenia</u> (additive effect when administered with <u>NRTIs</u>)<br><br>* <u>Nephrotoxicity</u><br><br>* Gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., <u>nausea</u>)<br><br>* <u>CNS</u><br><br>* <u>Headache</u><br><br>* Confusion<br><br>* <u>Paresthesias</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Mutation of viral UL97 <u>kinase</u><br><br> |
| Foscarnet | <br><br>* <u>Pyrophosphate</u> analogue<br><br>* Inhibition of <u>DNA</u>/<u>RNA polymerase</u> and <u>HIV</u> <u>reverse transcriptase</u> → direct inhibition of viral <u>DNA polymerases</u> via attachment to the <u>pyrophosphate</u>-binding site of the enzyme<br><br>* Does not require activation by viral <u>kinase</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ganciclovir</u>-resistant <u>CMV retinitis</u> in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u> (e.g., patients with <u>AIDS</u>)<br><br>* <u>Acyclovir</u>-resistant <u>HSV</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Nephrotoxicity</u><br><br>* Gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., <u>nausea</u>)<br><br>* <u>CNS</u><br><br>* <u>Headache</u><br><br>* Confusion<br><br>* <u>Seizures</u> due to <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities (e.g., <u>hypocalcemia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>)<br><br>* <u>Paresthesias</u><br><br>* Hematological abnormalities <br><br>* <u>Leukopenia</u><br><br>* <u>Neutropenia</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Mutation of viral <u>DNA polymerase</u><br><br> |
| Cidofovir | <br><br>* Viral <u>DNA polymerase</u> inhibitor with a long <u>half-life</u><br><br>* Direct inhibition of viral <u>DNA polymerases</u><br><br>* Does not require activation by viral <u>kinase</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>CMV retinitis</u> in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u> (e.g., patients with <u>AIDS</u>)<br><br>* <u>Acyclovir</u>-resistant <u>HSV</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Nephrotoxicity</u> (reduced with administration of <u>probenecid</u> and <u>IV fluids</u>)<br><br> |  |
| Fomivirsen | <br>* <u>Antisense</u> antiviral that blocks <u>translation</u> of viral <u>mRNA</u><br><br> | <br>* Local <u>treatment of CMV</u> retinitis in patients with <u>AIDS</u> (intraocular injection)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Eye</u> infections<br><br>* Increase in <u>intraocular pressure</u><br><br>* <u>Macular edema</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Unknown<br><br> |

## Antivirals against influenza viruses

| <br>Overview of antivirals against influenza viruses [[6]](/library/UA0bQi)[[7]](/library/2A0TQi)[[8]](/library/bXYH9n)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agents | Mechanism of action | Indications | Adverse effects |
| <br>Amantadine Rimantadine<br> | <br><br>* M2 ion channel blocker<br><br>* Weak <u>NMDA receptor antagonist</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Susceptible <u>influenza A</u> strains; all currently circulating strains are resistant and, therefore, treatment with adamantanes is not recommended<br><br>* <u>Parkinson disease</u>: See “<u>Medication for Parkinson disease</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Neurological<br><br>* <u>Ataxia</u><br><br>* <u>Anxiety</u><br><br>* Gastrointestinal<br><br>* <u>Nausea</u><br><br>* <u>Vomiting</u><br><br>* <u>Skin</u>: <u>livedo reticularis</u><br><br>* Other: <u>peripheral edema</u><br><br>* <u>Amantadine</u> only<br><br>* Orthostatic dysregulation<br><br>* <u>QT interval</u> prolongation<br><br><br> |
| <br>Oseltamivir  Zanamivir Peramivir<br> | <br>* Neuraminidase inhibitor: inhibition of progeny release from the surface of infected host cells<br><br> | <br><br>* Treatment of <u>influenza A</u> and B (reduces symptom duration if taken within 1–2 days of symptom onset)<br><br>* Prophylaxis of <u>influenza</u> in adults and pediatric patients ≥1 year (<u>oseltamivir</u>) and ≥ 5 years (<u>zanamivir</u>) of age<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Pulmonary: <u>upper respiratory tract infections</u><br><br>* Gastrointestinal<br><br>* <u>Nausea</u><br><br>* <u>Vomiting</u><br><br>* Other: <u>headache</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Baloxavir marboxil<br> | <br>* Viral <u>RNA polymerase</u> <u>endonuclease</u> inhibitor: blocks the <u>endonuclease</u> of the viral <u>RNA polymerase</u> → <u>endonuclease</u> cannot remove the <u>5' cap</u> from host <u>RNA</u> (a process referred to as cap snatching) → without the <u>5' cap</u> primer, the viral <u>RNA polymerase</u> cannot synthesize <u>RNA</u> → ↓ viral replication<br><br> | <br>* Treatment of <u>influenza A</u> and B (reduces symptom duration if taken within 48 hours of symptom onset)<br><br> | <br><br>* Gastrointestinal<br><br>* <u>Nausea</u><br><br>* <u>Diarrhea</u><br><br>* Pulmonary: <u>bronchitis</u><br><br>* Other: <u>headache</u><br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> In <u>influenza A</u> and B, administration of <u>neuraminidase inhibitors</u> within 2 days of symptom onset is vital to reduce the duration of illness and alleviate symptoms.
